title: Early hominin control of fire
summary: Controlling fire was a crucial turning point in human evolution, but there is no consensus on when it began. The earliest secure evidence for burning in an archaeological setting is burned bone and ashed plant remains from about 1 million years ago at Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa. The earliest hearths date to the time of Homo erectus, and were used for cooking, warmth and keeping predators away.

uncertainty.note: Wonderwerk Cave early Acheulean strata are dated to approximately 1.0 Ma; earlier traces around 1.5–1.8 Ma remain debated.

as_recorded.value: Between about 1.89 million and 110,000 years ago

where.modern_name: Wonderwerk Cave, Northern Cape, South Africa (earliest secure evidence; origin unlocated)
where.historical_name: Wonderwerk Cave, Kuruman Hills, southern Africa (Pleistocene early Acheulean site; no polity exists)

importance.justification: Controlled use of fire for cooking, warmth, and protection revolutionized hominin energetic efficiency, social structure, and technological capability across the genus Homo.

related.because: Cooked food provided higher caloric yields and metabolic energy that supported accelerated encephalization leading to early Homo sapiens.
